newsitem.title: USA: No EEP for grain now, more likely for value-added.
newsitem.headline: No EEP for grain now, more likely for value-added.

text.p: There is no need to employ export subsidies on U.S. grain sales at present, the Agriculture Department sales manager said Thursday, but added that European subsidies on flour sales were "very much under review."
Sales manager Chris Goldthwait told a House Agriculture subcommittee hearing prospects were "somewhat higher" for use of export subsidies on value-added products.
Asked by reporters if subsidies might be used to aid U.S. wheat flour exports, Goldthwait reiterated that European Union flour subsidies were being examined by USDA.
Goldthwait also told lawmakers that freeze damage to the winter wheat crop in the southern plains had reduced likelihood of a large harvest this year.

"Unfortunately, with the weather developments in recent weeks, it doesn't look terribly optimistic," Goldthwait said. "We had been hoping we would see a return to a more ample supply...Those hopes are dimmer."

Keeping the tight U.S. wheat supply in mind, Goldthwait said the United States had "sold just about everything we have to sell...We did not think it was prudent to reintroduce use of the export subsidy."

Several lawmakers asked Goldthwait to justify the Export Enhancement Program, the major U.S. export subsidy program, had not been used for wheat since July 1995. Subcommitte chairman Bill Barrett, Nebraska Republican, asked why there was "still no movement to crank up what has been a successful program."
"The program is ready to go if needed," Goldthwait said, but for now, there was "frankly no reason to buy down the price a few dollars a tonne when we are selling as much" as expected.
"This season, with respect to wheat, we believe they are wasting their dollars," he said when asked about EU export subsidies.
The United States will hold a smaller share of the world wheat market because of its tight supply, Goldthwait said.
"It has been our judgement...reintroducing EEP will not buy us additional market share for wheat," he said.
Afterward, Goldthwait told reporters USDA was watching EU subsidies on wheat flour -- "we have that very much under review" but declined to say if retaliation was likely.

In sizing up the wheat market, Goldthwait said it appeared "prices and demand may remain relatively strong for wheat in coming months." Old-crop and new-crop prices are at similar levels, he said. more
"The situation may be somewhat different when we go down the road a bit for some of the value-added products," Goldthwait said.
He cautioned there had been No USDA decision but there could be "use of the (EEP) program for some of the processed commodities."
As in recent months, Goldthwait said U.S. use of its export subsidies would be determined in part by EU behavior.

The National Association of Wheat Growers urged "reactivation of the EEP in time for the new marketing year" to prevent a long-term decline in U.S. market share. NAWG said it was disappointed there had been no action yet on EEP sales.
